The Chapter of the King and the Bird Qubbara,
The King said to the Philosopher: “I have heard the parable of the man who is surrounded by his enemies;
who seeks the help of one against the other and reconciles with him, so that he can be delivered, through it, from what he had feared; and who
keeps his promise and is saved. Present to me, if you will, the parable about harm inflicted, and those
who need to be wary of one another. The Philosopher said: “They claim that some King
called Barhamūd had a bird called Qubbara, who
could talk, was smart, and had a nestling. The King ordered that Qubbara and his nestling be taken to
a place where a woman who was the lady over all the women, was, and ordered her to take good care of him.
The King’s wife gave birth to a male child, and as he grew up, the nestling accustomed to the child.
They played together and ate with one another. Qubbara used to go to the mountain every day and bring
two items of an unknown fruit. He fed one to his nesting and one to the King’s child.
This accelerated their growth and increased their strength. The King noticed this, and it made Qubbarah, to him, more
distinguished-until a day came when Qubbara was away, getting the two items of that fruit:
the nestling jumped into the child’s lap. This angered the child, and he threw the nestling to
the ground, killing him. When Qubbara came and saw that his nestling had been killed, he was grieved and cried out, saying,
‘Shame on Kings who cannot be trusted and do not keep their promises; and woe to him who is put to test with their company!’
